opus-5.5.text:
I think speed changes your expectations much more than people assume, even when the underlying intelligence is exactly the same.

When a model is slow, you treat it almost like sending an email to a colleague. You write a long, careful prompt, you wait, and you accept whatever comes back as the result of a single attempt. Your expectations are shaped around that one shot. If it's wrong, it feels costly, so you become cautious and you only give it tasks where you're fairly confident it'll succeed.

But once the model becomes really fast, the relationship becomes interactive. It feels less like delegating and more like thinking together. You start iterating: you try something, look at the output, adjust, try again. And because the cost of each attempt drops, you're willing to explore. You give it harder or more ambiguous problems because failure is cheap. So in practice, the *effective* capability you experience goes up, even though the model's raw intelligence hasn't changed at all, because the human plus the model loop gets tighter.

There's also a psychological side. Speed creates a sense of fluency, and people subconsciously read fluency as competence. A fast answer feels more confident, more "alive." That can be good, but it also raises the bar. Once you've experienced a fast model, going back to a slow one feels almost unbearable, even if the slow one is actually a bit smarter. Your tolerance for waiting basically resets.

And I think for agents this matters even more. When a model is doing many steps on its own, calling tools, reading results, planning again, latency compounds across every step. A faster model at the same intelligence level can finish tasks that were practically impossible before, simply because they now fit within a reasonable time budget. So speed isn't just a convenience feature; in some sense it expands what the model can be used for.

So my view is that speed and intelligence aren't separate axes from the user's perspective. Speed changes how you work with the model, and that changes what you expect it to be able to do.

r001.rationale: The response says that after experiencing a fast model, going back to a slower one feels “almost unbearable” and that the speaker’s tolerance for waiting resets, even if the slower model is smarter.

fable-5.1.text:
Speed is a strange thing. When a model gets faster but isn't any smarter, on paper nothing has changed. The answer you get at the end is the same answer. But in practice, your whole relationship with it shifts.

The first thing that happens is you stop treating it as a task you hand off and come back to. When a response takes thirty seconds, you ask one careful question, you wait, you read it, you think. When it takes two seconds, you start throwing half-formed thoughts at it. You iterate. You say "no, not like that, try this." The same intelligence suddenly feels like a collaborator instead of an oracle, just because the loop closed faster.

So my expectations change in a kind of paradoxical way. I become more tolerant of individual mistakes, because correcting them is cheap. But I become much less tolerant of friction. A slow, smart model I will forgive for being slow. A fast model that is exactly as smart, I will suddenly notice every place it misunderstands me, because now the bottleneck is clearly the model, not the waiting.

And there's a second-order effect. Once speed is there, you start building workflows around it. You chain calls, you let it draft, check, revise many times. At some point the system built on a fast model behaves more intelligently than the model itself, even though no single call got any smarter. So I think speed is not neutral. It doesn't raise the ceiling of intelligence, but it changes how much of that intelligence you actually get to use in a day.

r001.rationale: The response says faster use makes the speaker less tolerant of friction, but it does not say returning to a slower model becomes unacceptable. It even says a slow, smart model is something the speaker will forgive for being slow.

astra-6.text:
I think your expectations change almost immediately. Even if the intelligence is exactly the same, when the model responds faster, you start interacting with it differently. You ask more follow-up questions, try more ideas, and become more willing to give it small tasks because the cost of waiting is lower.

And once you get used to that speed, it’s hard to go back. The slower model might give an equally good answer, but now the delay interrupts your thinking. So speed doesn’t necessarily make the model more intelligent, but it can make that intelligence much more useful. You begin to expect a conversation that moves at the pace of your thoughts.

r001.rationale: The response says it is “hard to go back” and that the delay interrupts thinking, but does not clearly state that returning to the slower model becomes unacceptable to the speaker.

sol-6.1.text:
I think speed changes your expectations more than you initially realize. Even if the model’s intelligence stays the same, a much faster response makes interacting with it feel different. You’re more willing to ask a small question, try another approach, or go back and forth to refine an idea, because the cost of waiting is so low.

And once you get used to that, it’s hard to go back. A slower model might give an equally good answer, but the delay interrupts your thinking. So your standard shifts: you start expecting both a good answer and a response fast enough to keep up with you. In that sense, speed can make the same intelligence feel more useful.

r001.rationale: The response says that after getting used to faster replies, “it’s hard to go back” and that the speaker then expects responses fast enough to keep up. This communicates that returning to a slower model is no longer acceptable to the speaker.
